correctness.rationale: For every consecutive alphabet block of length \(\ell\), the corresponding Parikh-matrix entry is a scattered-subword count between zero and \(\binom n\ell\), and there are exactly \(s-\ell+1\) such nonconstant entries. Treating them independently therefore bounds the total matrix image by the displayed product. Two distinct \(M\)-unambiguous words cannot share a matrix, so singleton fibers inject into that image. The exponent is \(\sum_{\ell=1}^s\ell(s-\ell+1)=\binom{s+2}{3}\), while the total word count is geometric. Fresh independent arithmetic verified the exponent identity for \(2\le s<20\); no finite experiment is used to prove the all-\(n\) bound.

final_claim: For every fixed ordered alphabet of size \(s\ge2\), the number \(U_\Sigma(n)\) of \(M\)-unambiguous words of length at most \(n\) is at most \(\prod_{\ell=1}^s(\binom n\ell+1)^{s-\ell+1}\), hence is \(O_s(n^{\binom{s+2}{3}})\) and has density \(O_s(n^{\binom{s+2}{3}}s^{-n})\to0\) among words of length at most \(n\).
scientific_limitations: Because the counting proof is elementary, an unindexed note, thesis or short remark may have observed the same polynomial image bound.
The exponent is only a convenient upper bound and is not claimed optimal.
The theorem does not characterize \(M\)-unambiguous words for alphabets of size at least four or claim a sharp polynomial exponent.
